Setup

import pandas as pd
import sqlite3

What is a database?

  • Information organized into tables (dataframes) and it may also include other structures related to those tables.
  • Within tables, data are organized as “records” and these “records” are related (or can be related).
  • Structured in a way so it can be easily accessed, managed, and updated.

What is a DBMS what is SQL?

  • A Database Management System (DBMS) is software
  • Commonly seen flavors are Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Postgres, SQLite
  • The software lets users interact with the database - query, modify, control access, etc.
  • SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to communicate with the DBMS

What is Python’s role?

  • Python can connect to SQL databases using libraries and/or database connectors that implement database standards.
Library Database Notes
sqlite3 SQLite Built into Python standard library
psycopg2 PostgreSQL Robust, https://pypi.org/project/psycopg2/
PyMySQL MySQL Pure Python implementation https://github.com/PyMySQL/PyMySQL
pyodbc MS SQL Server ODBC driver (additional software) required https://pypi.org/project/pyodbc/

Decisions, decisions

  • When do you choose to use SQL and when do you use Python?
  • I have already ported the database to Python, but let’s align with reality
Situation Choice
Large number of tables SQL is designed to handle complex joins efficiently and declaratively
You need only a subset of the data SQL can filter early (WHERE, JOIN ... ON, SELECT ...) — less data to load
You want to minimize memory usage SQL joins operate on disk; pandas loads everything into memory
The database schema is normalized SQL is optimized for normalized table designs with foreign keys
You want a single result table SQL can return a fully joined and clean result directly into pandas
You’ve already extracted small tables python/pandas joins are fast in-memory if data is small
You want to experiment interactively python/pandas easier to modify logic, write custom merge logic, or debug
You want to trace/inspect intermediate steps python/pandas is more transparent & readable step-by-step
Your joins are complex python/pandas in general allows much more flexibility

SQL Basics

General Readability Advice

  • Do make your SQL queries as readable, especially when they’re long.
    • Capitalize all SQL keywords to make them stand out,
    • Use line breaks and indentation to separate sections logically.
    • Use Aliases (using AS)
  • In this lecture, we can take advantage of Python until you are more comfortable with SQL

Example

  • readable SQL query with capitalized keywords and indentation
connection = sqlite3.connect("pokedex.sqlite")

query = f"""

SELECT 
    identifier, 
    color_id AS [color]

FROM pokemon_species

WHERE base_happiness > 50

ORDER BY identifier;
"""

readability_example = pd.read_sql(query, connection)

    PRIMARY KEY (id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(generation_id) REFERENCES generations (id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(evolves_from_species_id) REFERENCES pokemon_species (id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(evolution_chain_id) REFERENCES evolution_chains (id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(color_id) REFERENCES pokemon_colors (id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(shape_id) REFERENCES pokemon_shapes (id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(habitat_id) REFERENCES pokemon_habitats (id), 
    CHECK (is_baby IN (0, 1)), 
    CHECK (has_gender_differences IN (0, 1)), 
    FOREIGN KEY(growth_rate_id) REFERENCES growth_rates (id), 
    CHECK (forms_switchable IN (0, 1))
)

Using the Semicolon

  • The semicolon (;) is typically used to mark the end of a SQL query
  • SQLite3 does not require a semi-colon
  • Including a semi-colon improves readability
  • And compatibility across SQL implementations

Joins v Merge

SQL Join

  • Using JOIN to combine rows from related tables
  • Also demonstrating a subquery because of the complexity in the colors table
  • You could do this in pandas and not involve SQL
  • Default in SQL is an inner join

SQL Join Example

table_name1 = 'pokemon_species'
table_name2 = 'pokemon_color_names'
fields = 'sp.id, sp.identifier, sp.color_id, c.pokemon_color_id, c.name, sp.shape_id, sp.habitat_id, sp.base_happiness'
rule = 'sp.color_id = c.pokemon_color_id'

query = f"""

SELECT {fields}

FROM {table_name1} AS sp

JOIN (
    SELECT * FROM {table_name2}
    WHERE local_language_id = 9
) AS c ON {rule};
"""

SQL Join Result

join_result = pd.read_sql(query, connection)
join_result.rename(columns={"name": "color_name", "identifier": "species_name"}, inplace=True)

More About Joins

  • Common join types in SQLite are INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and CROSS JOIN.
  • SQLite does not support “ANTI JOIN” or even RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN directly
  • The solution is to turn to pandas

SQLite vs pandas joins

Feature SQLite pandas
INNER JOIN Yes Yes
LEFT JOIN Yes Yes
RIGHT JOIN No Yes
FULL OUTER JOIN No Yes
CROSS JOIN Yes Yes
ANTI JOIN Possible (need more code) Possible (needs filtering)

SQL Left Join

  • The habitat join is a good example for left join instead of the default inner
table_name1 = 'pokemon_species'
table_name2 = 'pokemon_habitat_names'
fields = 'sp.id, sp.identifier,  sp.habitat_id, h.pokemon_habitat_id, h.name, sp.shape_id,  sp.color_id,sp.base_happiness'
rule = 'sp.habitat_id =  h.pokemon_habitat_id'

query = f"""
SELECT {fields}
FROM {table_name1} AS sp
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT * FROM {table_name2}
    WHERE local_language_id = 9
) AS h ON {rule};
"""

SQL FULL OUTER JOIN

  • Simulated with UNION
  • Better to do this in pandas
table_name1 = 'pokemon_species'
table_name2 = 'pokemon_habitat_names'
fields = 'sp.id, sp.identifier,  sp.habitat_id, h.pokemon_habitat_id, h.name, sp.shape_id,  sp.color_id,sp.base_happiness'
rule = 'sp.habitat_id =  h.pokemon_habitat_id'
rule2 = 'h.pokemon_habitat_id = sp.habitat_id'

query = f"""
-- LEFT JOIN from species to habitat
SELECT {fields}
FROM {table_name1} AS sp
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT * FROM {table_name2}
    WHERE local_language_id = 9
) AS h ON {rule}

UNION

-- LEFT JOIN from habitat to species (simulating right join)
SELECT {fields}
FROM (
    SELECT * FROM {table_name2}
    WHERE local_language_id = 9
) AS h
LEFT JOIN {table_name1} AS sp ON {rule2}
WHERE sp.id IS NULL;
"""

SQL Full Outer Join result

# Load the two tables, correct issues

right.rename(columns={"pokemon_habitat_id": "habitat_id", "name": "habitat_name"}, inplace=True)

# Perform full outer join in pandas
merged = pd.merge(left, right, how="outer", on="habitat_id")

Group By

  • GROUP BY clause is used to aggregate rows
  • ORDER BY sorts the result, ascending is the default
query = """
SELECT 
    color_id, 
    COUNT(*)
FROM pokemon_species
GROUP BY color_id
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;
"""

GROUP BY with HAVING

  • HAVING clause is like WHERE but for grouped data results
query = """
SELECT 
    color_id, 
    COUNT(*)
FROM pokemon_species
GROUP BY color_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 50
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;
"""

Pattern Matching with LIKE

  • LIKE for partial matches with two types of wildcards:
    • % any sequence of characters (includes no characters).
    • _ represents a single character
  • LIKE is case-insensitive by default in SQLite

LIKE examples

query = """
SELECT *
FROM pokemon_species
WHERE identifier LIKE 'char%';
"""

pd.read_sql(query, connection)

LIKE examples

  • o is the fifth character out of OR u is the 7th character
  • parentheses separates the conditions
query = """
SELECT *
FROM pokemon_species
WHERE (identifier LIKE '____o' OR identifier LIKE '______u%') AND generation_id < 2;
"""

pd.read_sql(query, connection)

Additional SQLite

https://www.sqlite.org/lang.html

PRAGMA

  • https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html
  • The PRAGMA statement is an SQL extension specific to SQLite
  • They are used to modify the operation of the SQLite library or to query the SQLite library for internal (non-table) data
  • Unless you plan to regularly use SQLite as your version of SQL you might avoid PRAGMA solutions that you might find online
